stimulus.title: Natural Science: The Bacterial Chorus
stimulus.text:
For much of the twentieth century, bacteria were regarded as the ultimate loners. Each cell, according to the prevailing view, went about its business independently, absorbing nutrients, dividing, and responding to its surroundings without any regard for its neighbors. A colony of bacteria was simply a crowd of individuals that happened to be in the same place. That picture has changed dramatically. Researchers now know that many bacteria communicate with chemicals, and that by doing so they can act together in ways no single cell could manage.

Some of the earliest clues came from a glowing marine bacterium now called Vibrio fischeri. In laboratory cultures, scientists noticed something odd: when the bacteria were sparse, they produced no light at all, but when the population grew dense, the entire culture began to glow, more or less at once. Individual cells were clearly capable of producing light. Why would they wait until there were many of them to do it?

The answer turned out to involve a small molecule that each cell releases into its surroundings. When only a few bacteria are present, the molecule drifts away and its concentration stays low. As the population grows, more cells release more of the molecule, and its concentration rises. Once it passes a certain threshold, it triggers a change inside every cell: genes that had been switched off are switched on, and the cells begin to produce light. Because the signal reflects how many cells are nearby, researchers named the phenomenon quorum sensing, borrowing a term for the minimum number of members a group needs before it can make decisions.

Quorum sensing makes sense of a behavior that would otherwise seem wasteful. Producing light requires a great deal of energy. A single bacterium glowing in the open ocean would spend that energy for nothing, since its light would be far too faint to matter. But billions of bacteria glowing together can produce light bright enough to have an effect, and in the case of V. fischeri, that effect is put to use by an animal. The bacteria live inside a special organ of a small squid found in shallow Hawaiian waters. At night, the squid hunts near the surface, where moonlight from above would ordinarily cast its shadow downward, revealing it to predators below. The light produced by its bacterial partners is thought to cancel that shadow, helping to hide the squid. In return, the bacteria receive a protected, nutrient-rich home where they can reach the dense populations that switch on their glow.

Since the discovery of quorum sensing in light-producing bacteria, researchers have found that the strategy is remarkably widespread. Many bacteria use chemical signals to coordinate activities that pay off only when performed by large numbers of cells. Some disease-causing bacteria, for instance, appear to hold back the production of harmful substances until their numbers are large enough to overwhelm a host's defenses. Acting too early, when the population is small, might simply alert the immune system without accomplishing much.

That observation has opened an intriguing possibility for medicine. Most antibiotics work by killing bacteria or stopping their growth, and bacteria that survive a treatment can pass on whatever traits helped them survive, which over time produces resistant strains. Some researchers have proposed a different approach: rather than killing bacteria, interfere with their signals. If the bacteria never detect that they have reached a quorum, they may never launch the coordinated behaviors that make them dangerous. Because such a treatment would not directly threaten the bacteria's survival, some scientists have suggested that resistance might develop more slowly, though whether that hope will hold up in practice remains an open question.

Whatever its medical future, quorum sensing has changed how biologists think about the smallest forms of life. The notion of bacteria as solitary individuals has given way to a picture of populations that monitor, signal, and respond to one another. Even the simplest organisms, it turns out, may be listening to their neighbors.

stimulus.title: Natural Science: The Bacterial Chorus
stimulus.text:
For much of the twentieth century, bacteria were regarded as the ultimate loners. Each cell, according to the prevailing view, went about its business independently, absorbing nutrients, dividing, and responding to its surroundings without any regard for its neighbors. A colony of bacteria was simply a crowd of individuals that happened to be in the same place. That picture has changed dramatically. Researchers now know that many bacteria communicate with chemicals, and that by doing so they can act together in ways no single cell could manage.

Some of the earliest clues came from a glowing marine bacterium now called Vibrio fischeri. In laboratory cultures, scientists noticed something odd: when the bacteria were sparse, they produced no light at all, but when the population grew dense, the entire culture began to glow, more or less at once. Individual cells were clearly capable of producing light. Why would they wait until there were many of them to do it?

The answer turned out to involve a small molecule that each cell releases into its surroundings. When only a few bacteria are present, the molecule drifts away and its concentration stays low. As the population grows, more cells release more of the molecule, and its concentration rises. Once it passes a certain threshold, it triggers a change inside every cell: genes that had been switched off are switched on, and the cells begin to produce light. Because the signal reflects how many cells are nearby, researchers named the phenomenon quorum sensing, borrowing a term for the minimum number of members a group needs before it can make decisions.

Quorum sensing makes sense of a behavior that would otherwise seem wasteful. Producing light requires a great deal of energy. A single bacterium glowing in the open ocean would spend that energy for nothing, since its light would be far too faint to matter. But billions of bacteria glowing together can produce light bright enough to have an effect, and in the case of V. fischeri, that effect is put to use by an animal. The bacteria live inside a special organ of a small squid found in shallow Hawaiian waters. At night, the squid hunts near the surface, where moonlight from above would ordinarily cast its shadow downward, revealing it to predators below. The light produced by its bacterial partners is thought to cancel that shadow, helping to hide the squid. In return, the bacteria receive a protected, nutrient-rich home where they can reach the dense populations that switch on their glow.

Since the discovery of quorum sensing in light-producing bacteria, researchers have found that the strategy is remarkably widespread. Many bacteria use chemical signals to coordinate activities that pay off only when performed by large numbers of cells. Some disease-causing bacteria, for instance, appear to hold back the production of harmful substances until their numbers are large enough to overwhelm a host's defenses. Acting too early, when the population is small, might simply alert the immune system without accomplishing much.

That observation has opened an intriguing possibility for medicine. Most antibiotics work by killing bacteria or stopping their growth, and bacteria that survive a treatment can pass on whatever traits helped them survive, which over time produces resistant strains. Some researchers have proposed a different approach: rather than killing bacteria, interfere with their signals. If the bacteria never detect that they have reached a quorum, they may never launch the coordinated behaviors that make them dangerous. Because such a treatment would not directly threaten the bacteria's survival, some scientists have suggested that resistance might develop more slowly, though whether that hope will hold up in practice remains an open question.

Whatever its medical future, quorum sensing has changed how biologists think about the smallest forms of life. The notion of bacteria as solitary individuals has given way to a picture of populations that monitor, signal, and respond to one another. Even the simplest organisms, it turns out, may be listening to their neighbors.
